associate-foundations-mock3-5.task: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
associate-foundations-mock3-5.question: A support director wants to introduce Claude into the team's six-step ticket-triage process. Which sequencing is sound?

options.A: Automate all six steps in one rollout, then refine the prompts based on complaints
options.B: Start with one bounded, checkable step, prove it works with human review, then extend step by step
options.C: Begin with the hardest step, since most value is there and results will convince skeptics
options.D: Let each agent decide how to use Claude in triage and standardize on what spreads

associate-foundations-mock3-5.rationale: A bounded, checkable first step builds evidence and trust cheaply (B). Full automation at once (A) risks everything together, the hardest step (C) is least likely to succeed early, and uncoordinated adoption (D) produces inconsistency.
associate-foundations-mock3-5.evidence: Adoption guidance favors starting with scoped use cases and expanding once results are validated.

associate-foundations-mock3-6.task: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards
associate-foundations-mock3-6.question: A company policy forbids sending customer data to external services, and Claude has not been approved for such data. An agent wants Claude to summarize a customer's email thread. What applies?

options.A: The policy does not apply, because summarizing is processing rather than sending the data anywhere
options.B: The policy applies only if the email names the customer or lists account details
options.C: The policy does not apply, because the summary stays inside the company once it is produced
options.D: The policy applies, because pasting the email into Claude sends customer data externally

associate-foundations-mock3-6.rationale: Submitting the content is the act the policy governs (D). Calling it summarizing (A) or pointing to where the output ends up (C) misreads the policy, and it is not limited to named individuals (B).
associate-foundations-mock3-6.evidence: Organizational policy takes precedence over personal convenience; privacy guidance ties responsibility to what data is submitted.

associate-foundations-mock3-7.task: Understand the ethical implications of AI usage
associate-foundations-mock3-7.question: A sales director asks an analyst to send customers a Claude-written case study presented as written by the account team, with no mention of AI. The analyst is unsure. What is the right response?

options.A: Decline to present it as human-written, and raise disclosure with whoever is accountable for the relationship
options.B: Present it as the team's work, since customers judge the quality of a case study, not how it was produced
options.C: Present it as human-written after a colleague has reviewed it for accuracy, tone, and brand fit
options.D: Present it as human-written, and log the decision in the project file so it is traceable later

associate-foundations-mock3-7.rationale: Presenting AI output as human-written misrepresents its provenance, and the disclosure question belongs with whoever is accountable (A). Quality (B), a review pass (C), and an internal log (D) do not make the representation true.
associate-foundations-mock3-7.evidence: Claude's published values emphasize honesty and not creating false impressions about who or what produced content.

associate-foundations-mock3-8.task: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
associate-foundations-mock3-8.question: A strategy analyst asks Claude, 'What should we do about our declining renewal rate?' and gets a balanced discussion of options instead of a decision. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Claude cannot make recommendations on business matters, so it offers balanced discussion
options.B: The question was too short for Claude to infer which option would work best
options.C: The prompt never asked for one recommendation with its reasoning
options.D: The conversation had run long, and Claude hedges more as a chat gets longer

associate-foundations-mock3-8.rationale: Output shape follows the instruction, and no single recommendation was requested (C). Claude can recommend (A), length of the question (B) is not the variable, and chat length (D) does not explain a balanced format.
associate-foundations-mock3-8.evidence: Prompting guidance says to state the desired output explicitly, including what decision or format is expected.

associate-foundations-mock3-9.task: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
associate-foundations-mock3-9.question: A policy analyst needs a regulatory summary pitched at the right level for an executive committee that knows the business well but not the regulation. What is the most effective way to get that level?

options.A: Ask Claude to make the summary clear, well organized, and easy to scan
options.B: Ask for a shorter summary, since executives usually prefer brevity
options.C: Ask Claude to use simpler words and shorter sentences throughout
options.D: Name the audience and what they already know, and say which concepts to explain

associate-foundations-mock3-9.rationale: Naming the readers and their prior knowledge is what calibrates level (D). Clarity (A), length (B), and vocabulary (C) are side effects rather than the instruction that sets the level.
associate-foundations-mock3-9.evidence: Prompting guidance says to give context about the audience and purpose of the output.

associate-foundations-mock3-10.task: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
associate-foundations-mock3-10.question: A team lead notices a colleague uses the largest model for every task, including reformatting meeting notes into a table. What should she point out?

options.A: That it is harmless, because the extra capability costs nothing on simple tasks like this
options.B: That larger models are less accurate on simple formatting because they overthink it
options.C: That matching the model to the task cuts cost and waiting without hurting simple work
options.D: That every task should move to the smallest model to hold costs down

associate-foundations-mock3-10.rationale: Fit-to-task is the principle: simple work gains nothing from extra capability (C). Capability has a cost (A), larger models are not worse at simple tasks (B), and moving everything to the smallest model (D) overcorrects for harder work.
associate-foundations-mock3-10.evidence: Model guidance says to choose the model that meets quality needs at the lowest cost and latency.

associate-foundations-mock3-11.task: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
associate-foundations-mock3-11.question: Analysts have access to a strong model, yet usage is low because staff copy data between three systems to give Claude context and then retype its answers. Why would changing how people use Claude matter more than a stronger model?

options.A: The model sets the quality of every result, so changing the interface cannot change outcomes
options.B: The obstacle is how people supply context and act on output, not answer quality
options.C: Interface choice matters only once a team grows past a few dozen users
options.D: Interface matters only when the stronger model costs too much to roll out

associate-foundations-mock3-11.rationale: When the bottleneck is supplying context and acting on output, the interface dominates (B). Treating the model as decisive (A) misses that, and neither team size (C) nor cost (D) defines when interface matters.
associate-foundations-mock3-11.evidence: Product guidance describes connectors and integrations that bring context into Claude and fit it into existing tools.

associate-foundations-mock3-12.task: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
associate-foundations-mock3-12.question: A policy owner uploads the revised travel policy to a Project's knowledge but leaves the old version in place. What is the risk?

options.A: Answers can blend current rules with superseded ones, since both files stay retrievable
options.B: Claude will ignore the new file until the old one is deleted from the Project's knowledge
options.C: The Project will hit its storage limit and then stop accepting further questions
options.D: Claude will refuse to answer travel questions until the conflict is resolved

associate-foundations-mock3-12.rationale: Superseded material stays retrievable and contradicts the current version, so answers can blend the two (A). Claude does not ignore new files (B) or stop working over conflicts (C, D).
associate-foundations-mock3-12.evidence: Project knowledge should be kept current; outdated files remain available to Claude until removed.

associate-foundations-mock3-13.task: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
associate-foundations-mock3-13.question: A knowledge manager is deciding which team materials to add to a shared Project's knowledge. Which test is best?

options.A: Whether most of the Project's conversations would benefit from having it available
options.B: Whether the file is long enough to justify the effort of uploading it
options.C: Whether the file was created recently, so the Project reflects current work
options.D: Whether the file is confidential and so needs the Project's protection

associate-foundations-mock3-13.rationale: Recurring relevance across conversations is what separates shared knowledge from content that belongs in a single prompt (A). Length (B), recency (C), and sensitivity (D) are unrelated to that test.
associate-foundations-mock3-13.evidence: Projects hold context that applies across chats; one-off material belongs in the individual conversation.

associate-foundations-mock3-14.task: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
associate-foundations-mock3-14.question: A prompt that reliably produced half-page summaries now returns two-line answers, though nobody edited its wording. What should the owner check first?

options.A: Whether the model the team uses has been deprecated and now answers more tersely
options.B: Whether the inputs or instructions changed, including Project additions
options.C: Whether a slow network connection is cutting responses off before they finish
options.D: Whether the account has hit a usage limit that shortens replies to save capacity

associate-foundations-mock3-14.rationale: A behavior change points to a change in inputs or configuration, which is the cheapest thing to check (B). Deprecation (A), network speed (C), and limits (D) produce errors or delays rather than consistently shorter answers.
associate-foundations-mock3-14.evidence: Prompt-testing guidance says to compare against known-good inputs and configuration when results change.

associate-foundations-mock3-15.task: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
associate-foundations-mock3-15.question: A manager says Claude gave a colleague a wrong fact today that it had stated correctly last week. What is the most useful first question for the manager to ask?

options.A: Which model and plan were you using when it happened?
options.B: How long had the conversation been running by then?
options.C: What exactly did you ask, and what did Claude reply? Can you share the chat?
options.D: Did you try asking again to see whether the error repeats?

associate-foundations-mock3-15.rationale: The exact exchange is what makes the claim examinable (C). Model (A), conversation length (B), and retrying (D) may matter later, but none of them shows what actually happened.
associate-foundations-mock3-15.evidence: Prompt-testing guidance relies on concrete inputs and outputs to diagnose a failure.
